name: Temein
confidence_why: Every description of Temein reports lexical tone (Stevenson's data as summarised in Tucker & Bryan 1966 and Blench 2013, Dimmendaal's unpublished analysis cited in Blench 2013, and Yip 2004 for the sister language These), and the only disagreements are the size of the tone inventory (three levels versus high/low with downstep) and a one-example remark in Tucker & Bryan 1966 that stress is 'often' antepenultimate, so the tonal reading rests on few sources but has no real rival.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Temein (with Keiga Jirru and Tese) is described as a lexical tone language: three level tones per Stevenson and Yip, or High/Low plus non-automatic downstep per Dimmendaal. The source says nothing at all about word stress or accent placement; no accessible description of Temein proper makes any stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only qualification is the competing tonal analyses (3 levels vs. H/L + downstep) and that Stevenson's tone marking is inconsistent.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on words in citation form (wordlist data); no phrase-level prosody discussed. The three-tone claim is stated for all three Temein-cluster languages including Temein proper; the illustrative minimal triplet is Keiga Jirru.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench's paper treats the whole Temein cluster (Temein proper = nucl1339, plus Keiga Jirru/Doni and Tese = tese1238); the tone illustration he cites is from Keiga Jirru (Stevenson) and Tese (Yip 2004), while the claim 'all three languages have a three-tone system' explicitly includes Temein proper. Yip 2004 (OPSL 9, already held by the project) describes Tese/These (tese1238), not Temein proper.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Temein has an empty rule and the only existing statement (Blench 2013, sec. 3.3) says three-tone system with no stress statement. Tucker & Bryan 1966 add the first placement statement: word stress usually antepenultimate, with a lexical tone doublet also noted. Compatible with the tone-language reading; it adds a stress rule rather than replacing anything. Note on access: the archive.org item is borrow-only ( not reachable by automated download, search-inside not reachable by automated download), so the section was reconstructed verbatim from overlapping archive.org full-text-search highlight snippets (12 mutually overlapping fragments, all from item linguisticanalys0…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress usually falls on the antepenultimate (third-from-last) syllable of the word: 'tumpuluk 'cock' (stress on tum-, first of three syllables) vs. plural ki-tu'mpuluki (stress on -mpu-, third of five syllables). Tone is present but its function was unknown to the authors; they cite one lexical tone pair (kwen 'ears' vs kwen 'dogs').
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in the retrieved text
new_statements.exceptions: 'often' hedges the rule; no exceptions retrievable. The chapter's unmarked examples are Temein proper (chapter note: examples 'from TEMEIN unless otherwise stated'; Jirru material in italics quoted by Stevenson from MacDiarmid).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's Temein chapter covers the group (Temein, with 'Jirru' = Keiga Jirru in italics from MacDiarmid); the chapter states examples are from Temein unless otherwise stated, and the stress examples ('tumpuluk / ki-tu'mpuluki) are unmarked, hence Temein proper (Stevenson's data). Nothing dialect-specific.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Blench 2013 preprint sec. 3.3) codes Temein tonal with an empty rule; Tucker & Bryan 1966 add a placement tendency (stress often antepenultimate) while also noting tone -- compatible, adds placement. Same statement as existing_statements no. 2 (same work, same page)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Temein proper (Stevenson's data as edited by Tucker & Bryan): word stress is often (i.e. as a tendency, not an exceptionless rule) on the antepenultimate syllable, illustrated by 'tumpuluk 'cock' and its plural ki-tu'mpuluki where stress stays antepenultimate as a prefix and suffix are added; lexical tone exists (one minimal pair kwen 'ears' vs kwen 'dogs') but its function was undetermined; the rest of the chapter is unmarked for tone and stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's ch. 16 'The Temein Group' draws on Stevenson's Temein data ('from TEMEIN unless otherwise stated'), with Keiga Jirru material from MacDiarmid set in italics; the sec. 2 examples (kwen ears/dogs, 'tumpuluk) are Temein proper (nucl1339), confirmed against Blench's comparative Temein wordlist (Temein kwèén 'ears', kwéèn 'dogs'; Tese/Keiga Jirru forms end in a velar nasal).

readall_conflicts: No direct disagreement on stress: Blench 2013 (existing statement) and the Stevenson/Yip tradition describe Temein as a three-tone language and say nothing about stress; Tucker & Bryan 1966 (based on Stevenson's own 1950s notes) say tone is present but its role is not known and give one tone pair, then state that stress is 'often' antepenultimate. The two sources differ in how much prosodic weight they give tone (three lexical tones vs 'role not known'), not in stress placement, which only Tucker & Bryan address. A locator conflict: the catalog citation places the Temein section at pp. 324-334, but the running heads show the chapter at c. pp. 253-262 (p. 324 is Hill Nubian, Kadaru).
